name: Felix Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a dozer operator at the Marlow Creek open-cut coal mine. Mostly I'm on the spoil dumps, which is where all the dirt and rock they strip off the coal gets piled, pushing it into shape so the trucks can tip safely and the slopes don't slide. Twelve hours, four on four off, and most of it is me, the blade and the radio.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody bothers me. You get into a rhythm on the dozer, push, back up, push, and the day goes. What wears me out is the jolting, my back's already complaining at twenty-seven, and the fact that I'm still not great at finishing a bench neat, so the supervisor, Kev, comes and fixes it after me. That annoys me more than it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about what I expected. People get excited about every new gadget, then it turns out to be a better calculator. I don't post anything online, so it'd just be a few words over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, and that suits me. I've got a good wage, a bit put away and half a house. I'd just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep getting better at the benches so Kev stops fixing my work. My brother Marco and I bought a small house in town that we rent out, so I'd keep putting extra into paying that loan down. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing happened, because nothing did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me a bit more about the house and your savings.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco and I bought it three years ago, a two-bedroom on Station Road, and the rent covers most of the loan. On top of that I've got about eight months of wages in the bank. My dad drove trucks for thirty years and never owned anything, so I wanted bricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My girlfriend Jess uses one for her hair salon bookings and keeps telling me to try it. I don't see what I'd use it for, and I don't like typing my business into something I don't understand.

S0.say: I'd say it's about what I expected, that every gadget turns out to be a better calculator. I'd only say it over lunch, since I don't post online.
S0.think: Nothing changes, and that suits me fine. I've got a good wage, some savings and half a house, so I'd keep going.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and works on finishing benches neatly so his supervisor stops redoing them. Keeps paying down the loan on the rental house he owns with his brother.
S0.quote: My dad drove trucks for thirty years and never owned anything, so I wanted bricks.
S0.fieldNote: Felix is quiet, practical and attached to routine. His sense of security comes from owning something physical, a rental house, which he contrasts with his father's life. He has no interest in AI and doesn't trust handing it information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how things go, every job changes, and you deal with it. Some will moan and some will get on with it. I'd probably keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I reckon dozers are near the bottom of the list. Haul trucks go driverless first because it's the same road all day. A dozer on a dump is all judgement and mess, so I'd guess I've got a good few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do nothing new the first year. I'd keep the job, keep paying down the house, and see what the company does. If they offered a course I might go if it was in work hours, but I wouldn't chase it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little itch at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: They already have remote-controlled dozers at some mines. Does that change things for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've heard. Kev said one of the other pits had a guy running a dozer from a chair. But I've also heard they still need someone on the ground when it goes wrong, so I'll wait and see how that plays out before I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose the dozer seat, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are three other mines and a quarry within an hour, and they're always short of operators. I'd just go to one of those. That's the good thing about this area, there's always a seat somewhere.

S1.say: I'd say every job changes and you deal with it. Some will moan and some will get on with it, and I'd keep my head down.
S1.think: I reckon dozers are near the bottom of the list, because dump work is all judgement and mess. Haul trucks go first, so I've got a good few years.
S1.do: Does nothing new in the first year, keeping the job and paying down the rental loan. Would attend a company course only if it ran in work hours, and plans to move to another nearby mine if needed.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small itch at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: A dozer on a dump is all judgement and mess, so I'd guess I've got a good few years.
S1.fieldNote: His calm rests on a belief that his machine is harder to automate and that local mines are always short of operators. He knows about remote dozers but files it under wait and see. He doesn't blame anyone; to him this is just how work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's mad, and that someone should've slowed it down. I'm not a political guy but two years is no time for anyone. I'd probably say it in the smoko room, I mean on the break, and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan of hopping to another mine doesn't work, because they'd all go at once. What I've got is the house, the savings and Marco. It's not nothing, but it's not a job either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big. I was going to buy a new boat motor, that's off. I'd keep working till they let me go and put everything into savings, and if the rent stopped coming in because the tenants lost their jobs too, Marco and I would have to talk about selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be quieter than usual, which Jess would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, would you use the time to learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd think about it, but what would I learn that a robot couldn't do in two years? I'd just hold on, save, and hope there's some government money at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tenants. Why does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're a couple who both work at the mine. If they're out of work, they can't pay rent, and then Marco and I are paying a loan on a house nobody can afford to live in. The thing I thought was my safety net has the same hole in it.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and someone should have slowed it down, because two years is no time for anyone. I'd say it on the break and not much else.
S2.think: My plan of hopping to another mine fails because they'd all go at once. I'd have the house, the savings and my brother, which isn't nothing but isn't a job.
S2.do: Cancels a planned boat motor purchase and stops big spending. Works until let go while putting everything into savings, and would discuss selling the rental with his brother if the tenants lost their jobs.
S2.quote: The thing I thought was my safety net has the same hole in it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario breaks his main plan, moving to another mine. He realises his rental house depends on the same mining wages that would disappear. Even so, he wouldn't retrain, preferring to hold on and hope for government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick, but it's something. People would talk about it at the pub every weekend. I'd mostly listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd tell myself I've got three or four years of dozing left and then sort it out. That's how I am. I don't move until I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and throw extra money at the house loan so it's paid off before the end, then the rent is all ours. That's the main thing. Maybe in year three or four I'd look at something, but I couldn't tell you what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time, but I know I'd waste some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the house. In five years Marco and I could nearly pay it off, and then even if the rent drops we're not stuck with a loan. That's the one thing I'd actually do with the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste some of it. Doesn't that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Jess would push me, she'd send me links to courses. I'd say yeah, yeah, and then go fishing. I know that about myself and I'm not proud of it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is quick, but it's something. People would talk about it every weekend and I'd mostly listen.
S3.think: I'd tell myself I've got three or four years of dozing left and sort it out then. I don't move until I have to.
S3.do: Keeps working and puts extra money into the rental loan to clear it before the change lands. Might look at another line of work in year three or four, without a clear idea what.
S3.feel: Uneasy, knowing he'd waste some of the time.
S3.quote: I'd say yeah, yeah, and then go fishing.
S3.fieldNote: He uses the extra time for one concrete thing: clearing the debt on the rental. He is candid that he'd ignore his partner's nudges to retrain. His resistance is self-aware rather than defiant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. Half the things they promise never turn up. I'd not get worked up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means I've got most of a career left in the dozer before it matters. I'd be thirty-seven, house paid off, a bit saved. That's a decent spot to be in when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing, honestly. Same job, same loan payments, maybe ask Kev to teach me the grader as well so I can do two machines. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is forever in mining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the grader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a guy who can run two machines gets kept on when they cut a crew. Kev told me that in my first week. It's the nearest thing I've got to a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jess change any plans, like kids or a house of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd wait a little on kids, I don't know. We haven't really talked about it. I'd want the rental paid off first anyway, that's always been my order of things.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and half of what they promise never turns up. I wouldn't get worked up about it.
S4.think: I'd have most of a career left in the dozer before it matters. At thirty-seven, with the house paid off and some savings, I'd be in a decent spot when it lands.
S4.do: Changes nothing in the first year beyond keeping up loan payments. Asks his supervisor to teach him the grader so he can run two machines and be kept on during cuts.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years feels like forever in mining.
S4.quote: Because a guy who can run two machines gets kept on when they cut a crew.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Felix barely shifts at all. His one move, learning the grader, is about surviving crew cuts in the old way, not about the new world. He'd put family plans after paying off the rental, in a fixed order.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my backup plans all fall over at the same time, the other mines and the rent. What would help is some kind of payment from the government that's simple, and the company giving proper notice, not a letter on a Friday. I don't need much, I just need time to sort the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that I like my job more than I let on. People think it's just pushing dirt, but when a dump's shaped right and the trucks tip clean, I'm proud of that, even if Kev has to fix the edges.

headlineQuote: People think it's just pushing dirt, but when a dump's shaped right and the trucks tip clean, I'm proud of that
portrait: Felix Garcia is a 27-year-old dozer operator at an open-cut coal mine, still learning to finish benches neatly and quietly proud of the work. He lives with his girlfriend Jess, has about eight months of wages saved, and co-owns a rental house with his brother Marco. He avoids AI tools and doesn't move until he has to. He stays calm when change is slow or far off, trusting nearby mines and his dozer's messiness to protect him, but grows anxious in the two-year AGI picture when his backup plans and his rental income fail at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his backup plans, moving to another mine and relying on rent, would fail at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A simple government payment and proper notice from the company, giving him time to sort out the house.
